items.fullText: The Wizard of Open Weights: Chris Alexiuk Makes AI Easy With Open Models With a parakeet, a webcam and a conviction that AI belongs to everyone — how one NVIDIAN became NVIDIA Nemotron’s loudest advocate. November 5, 2026 by Matthew Leib 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! Chris Alexiuk has a simple rule about open source AI: If you believe in it, be loud about it. “We should be shouting about this technology from the rooftops,” said Alexiuk, a Toronto-based senior product research engineer in deep learning at NVIDIA who specializes in making open large language models (LLMs) practical for working developers. Alexiuk’s preferred “rooftop” is YouTube , where he’s built a following teaching curious thousands how to build, fine-tune, evaluate and ship production LLM applications and agents. “I think the people who will most help us understand how to build and apply AI likely haven’t even heard of it yet,” he said. “Trying to get knowledge and information out to as many people as humanly possible is what continues to drive me.” Bringing NVIDIA Nemotron to Developers Everywhere Having spent years teaching developers to build with open models, Alexiuk has concluded that transparency isn’t a feature of good AI; it’s the precondition for it. “Fully open source AI is necessary for the democratization of intelligence,” he said. “You should have access to the weights, the data that went into it, the training recipes, everything.” That’s why, on his LinkedIn profile, Alexiuk styles himself “No. 1 Nemotron Fan,” referring to the NVIDIA Nemotron family of open source, multimodal models built for long-running, self-evolving and specialized AI agents. “I think Nemotron is the most important project that exists,” said Alexiuk, who also uses the pseudonym “Joe Nemotron” across social media. “I’m a firm believer that openness is a very important thing to undertake, so I’m going to be the No. 1 fan of whoever is doing that the best. items.fullText: More Performance From Every Byte: How Full-Stack Codesign Solves AI’s Memory Challenge November 5, 2026 by Amr Elmeleegy 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! Larger models, longer contexts and agentic applications are increasing GPU memory pressure while supply tightens and prices rise — a trend expected to continue through the near term. NVIDIA works closely with memory partners to rapidly adopt the latest memory technologies. NVIDIA was first to adopt HBM3e and HBM4 technologies into an accelerated computing stack. But the approach isn’t to simply pack more memory onto the GPU. It’s full-stack codesign. NVIDIA intentionally designs GPUs, CPUs, networking, storage and software together to get more useful work out of memory at every layer of the AI factory. That matters because an AI factory runs on a memory and storage hierarchy. GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM) is the fastest, most expensive and most contested tier — with model weights and KV cache competing for limited capacity. Below it sit CPU memory, local SSDs and shared storage, each trading speed for more capacity at a lower cost per bit. How much useful work a byte does depends on how well the whole hierarchy is used: shrinking what must be stored, placing it on the right tier and bringing it back to the GPU before it’s needed. Byte for byte, NVIDIA makes the most efficient use of memory at every layer — and the results show it. From NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra to the Vera Rubin platform, HBM capacity per GPU rose roughly 3%, while agentic throughput per dollar rose by up to 30x on SemiAnalysis AgentX. Agentic Inference Is Putting More Pressure on HBM Frontier models now have trillions of parameters — the values that hold what an AI model learned in training. KV cache, which holds the context the model needs to understand each active request without reprocessing the same information, is also expanding. items.fullText: Cities Worldwide Build and Scale AI Services With NVIDIA Physical and Agentic AI From infrastructure planning and transportation to public services, cities are using NVIDIA-powered applications to address local needs and expand capacity for the broader AI ecosystem. November 2, 2026 by Esther Lee 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! Cities generate enormous amounts of data from cameras, sensors and operational systems, but turning it into useful action — for planning, maintenance and public services — remains a challenge. Physical and agentic AI offer new ways to close that gap, from digital twins for infrastructure planning to vision and service agents, while keeping local governments in control of how sensitive data is processed and used. Building on initiatives announced at GTC Berlin , NVIDIA and its partners are expanding physical AI and AI agents to cities worldwide. Shared computing infrastructure gives city departments, neighboring municipalities and local developers a common foundation to build on — extending services without each organization having to acquire and manage resources of their own. Agentic AI for Cities From resident services to vision agents, cities are adopting NVIDIA agentic AI to deliver faster, more responsive public services. City teams don’t need a massive infrastructure investment to get started building these AI services: depending on the workload, NVIDIA RTX workstations or a small GPU system may be enough. In Spain, 1MillionBot combines open source ALIA models trained at the Barcelona Supercomputing Center with NVIDIA Nemotron and other models in resident-service agents for Madrid Digital (Comunidad de Madrid), Administració Oberta de Catalunya and 150+ deployments across Spain, handling municipal procedures, appointment requests, urban-planning incidents and service inquiries. items.fullText: NVIDIA Unveils Minerva to Bring End-to-End Observability for AI Factories New AIOps platform connects infrastructure and workload telemetry to help operators increase uptime and maximize AI factory yield. October 22, 2026 by Brian Sparks 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! Launched today, NVIDIA Minerva is an AIOps platform built to help teams find problems earlier and keep AI factories productive. It brings together telemetry from infrastructure and AI workloads, then applies purpose-built AI models to turn that data into timely, actionable insight. AI factories are among the most complex operations in the world, with vast numbers of GPUs working across high-speed networks to train models and serve AI applications. At that scale, a single degraded component can slow an entire job. The warning signs may be easy to miss, such as a GPU running hotter than its peers or an NVMe drive losing performance under load. The platform focuses on AI factory yield, a measure of the useful work infrastructure produces through GPU hours, goodput, cluster uptime and token production. Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements Delivering a Dynamic View of an AI Factory Traditional monitoring tools often divide the data center into separate views. Networking, compute, site reliability and machine learning teams each see a different part of the operation. Minerva connects those signals across NVIDIA GPUs, networking, storage, schedulers and workloads. With these signals, Minerva builds a dynamic knowledge graph that logically maps the infrastructure — GPUs, SuperNICs, switches and cables — and the jobs running on it. This context helps operators trace a slow training job to the component affecting it, even across a factory with hundreds of thousands of GPUs. items.fullText: How Companies Are Using NVIDIA DSX to Break the Power Bottleneck Companies around the world are using the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform to plan, simulate and run AI factories as one system and unlock infrastructure development. October 21, 2026 by Vladimir Troy 0 Comments Share Share This Article X Facebook LinkedIn Copy link Link copied! Companies around the world are building on the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform to plan, simulate and run the grid and the AI factory as one system, from the substation to the rack. Their adoption of the platform responds to an acute problem. Power is now the biggest bottleneck in infrastructure. More than $300 billion in equipment is backlogged, and over 200 gigawatts of projects are waiting in U.S. interconnection queues. One root cause of the bottleneck is siloed systems. The grid, the facility and the compute inside have long been designed independently from one another, creating the conditions for delays, risk and stranded capacity. Read All NVIDIA in Europe Announcements To help address this, NVIDIA DSX brings these systems together: NVIDIA DSX Sim and SimReady assets from leading energy manufacturers let engineers simulate the grid, substation and AI factory together, validating generators, switchgear, power systems and cooling before breaking ground. NVIDIA DSX Flex syncs AI factory demand with grid conditions and onsite generation, turning AI factories from static loads into flexible grid assets. NVIDIA DSX MaxLPS and DSX Exchange squeeze more compute from every watt and securely share signals across compute, networking, energy, cooling and operations. GE Vernova is deploying its grid-to-facility and rack power expertise to complement NVIDIA DSX systems, enabling customers to transform power constraints into competitive advantages while maximizing compute and token output, sustainability and grid reliability.
